rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to retain early compounds while promoting elution of all 10 compounds within the acquisition window. The retention and resolution pattern will guide targeted optimization of gradient range, duration, and temperature.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing whether the substantial resolution margin survives. Keep composition endpoints and temperature fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.
The 10-minute gradient eliminates the time penalty but compresses a central peak cluster. Test a substantial temperature change to alter selectivity while retaining the faster gradient.

Back away from the high-temperature co-elution and modestly lengthen the gradient to improve separation within the central cluster. This combination should keep the last peak relatively early while testing for full resolution.
Slightly reduce gradient steepness to test whether the narrow resolution margins can improve while preserving a negligible time penalty. Injection 4 remains the established maximum-score method.

Test a 5 °C decrease from injection 4 to assess temperature sensitivity and seek larger critical-pair resolution margins. The maximum CRF is already established; this run explores a neighboring method that may also retain a zero time penalty.

Return to the successful 55 °C temperature and test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention while changing gradient selectivity. This explores whether another maximum-score method exists with better critical-pair resolution margins.

Reduce the final organic fraction to recover resolution for the limiting pair in injection 7. The slightly shallower gradient may bring all pairs above 1.5 while keeping the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window.

A further small decrease in gradient steepness should lift the limiting resolution above 1.5 while preserving separation of the other critical pair. The last peak is expected near 8 minutes, close to the zero-time-penalty boundary.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with the faster gradient, since the high-scoring region around 55 °C is already mapped. Cooling may separate the central cluster through a different elution pattern, although increased retention could introduce a time penalty.

Test the upper-temperature neighbor of the maximum-score method to complete the local temperature comparison. The longer gradient may relieve the near-co-elution seen at 60 °C with the 10-minute gradient while maintaining a zero time penalty.

Test whether the successful 55 °C selectivity supports a shorter gradient without losing full resolution. This isolates gradient duration relative to injection 4 and could identify a faster method with the same maximum CRF.

Use a gradient slope between injections 8 and 9, where the limiting resolution crossed 1.5. This should preserve full separation with the last peak slightly earlier than injection 9, potentially matching the maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to balance shorter retention against central-pair separation. This explores whether the maximum-score region extends beyond the starting compositions tested so far.

Test whether higher starting organic content improves the central-pair separation that was limiting at 50 °C, while the lower temperature separates the pair limiting injection 14. This explores a different selectivity balance; the established CRF 1.000 methods remain the benchmarks.

Preserve injection 4’s successful gradient slope but stop the ramp at 0.65 organic after 8 minutes. Since all peaks previously eluted by 7.60 minutes, this should reproduce the maximum-score separation with a lower final organic fraction.

Keep the successful gradient slope but transition to the final hold after the first nine peaks have eluted. This tests whether a lower final organic fraction can preserve CRF 1.000 without delaying the last peak beyond the zero-time-penalty window.

Slightly flatten the gradient relative to injection 13 to improve its limiting pair while retaining the other critical separation. Injection 17 shows that a last-peak time of 8.35 minutes still incurs no time penalty, leaving room for this adjustment to match CRF 1.000.

Use a shallower gradient to recover the central-pair resolution lost at the higher starting composition in injection 14. This tests whether increased resolution margins are attainable before the longer retention introduces a time penalty.

Reduce the gradient slope slightly from injection 19 to lift its limiting resolution above 1.5 while maintaining the other critical pair’s margin. The last peak is expected near 9 minutes, testing whether this starting composition can also achieve the maximum CRF without a time penalty.

Preserve injection 9’s gradient slope while lowering the endpoint and shortening the programmed ramp. The gradient ends at the outlet at 8.65 minutes, after the previously observed last peak at 8.00 minutes, so this should retain CRF 1.000.

Test a slightly shallower gradient and lower endpoint than injection 21 to increase the earlier critical pair’s resolution margin. The later critical pair should remain resolved, while the last peak is expected near the upper edge of the zero-time-penalty window.
Match injection 4’s successful gradient slope with a shorter ramp and lower endpoint. Because the ramp still extends beyond the last peak, this should reproduce the established maximum CRF of 1.000.
Use a gradient slope between the maximum-score conditions of injections 9 and 18. This should retain full resolution and a zero time penalty while testing a higher final organic fraction.

Test a shallower gradient at the successful starting composition and temperature, targeting full resolution near the 9-minute zero-time-penalty boundary. The maximum CRF of 1.000 is already established; this final run probes the edge of that operating region.
